ety.text: Etymology tree Sanskrit आख्याति (ākhyāti) Prakrit अक्खइ (akkhaï) Hindi आखना Inherited from Prakrit अक्खइ (akkhaï, “say”), from Sanskrit आख्याति (ākhyāti). Related to आख्या (ākhyā), आख्यान (ākhyān), बखान (bakhān, “narrative”), पखाना (pakhānā, “report, story”).

f: ایک ہاتھ سے تالی نہیں بجتی

ety.text: Inherited from Proto-New Indo-Aryan *एड्डि (ĕḍḍi). See एड़ी (eṛī).
Deverbal form of कटना (kaṭnā) with the suffix -आई (-āī).
Borrowed from Classical Persian قَبْضَه (qabza, “property, fist, power”), from Arabic قَبْضَة (qabḍa, “clutch, fist, authority”).

s.g: a flourishing or thriving place, a place with liveliness and satisfaction, a lush or verdant place
Chaman (a city in Qilla Abdullah district, Balochistan, Pakistan)

x: अबे चमन सरताज विद्रोह और लोकतांत्रिक चुनावों में तुम्हें कोई फ़र्क ही नहीं दिखा
अबे चमन उस समय 1GB डेटा एक महिना जाता था अभी आधा दिन भी नही जाता है

ety.text: Clipping of चमन चूतिया (caman cūtiyā, “absolute moron, idiot”), in which expression चमन (caman, “garden”) acts as an intensifier.

x: चित्र दीवार पे लटक रहा है।
इस चित्र को परिवर्द्धित करना पड़ेगा।
यह चित्र मेरी आँखों गड़ गया।

ety.text: Borrowed from Sanskrit चित्र (citrá). Doublet of चीता (cītā) and चेहरा (cehrā)

s.g: to eat a meal, to dine

ety.text: Derived from Sanskrit जेमति (jemati), जमति (jamati), possibly from Proto-Munda *ɟv₁₀m (“to eat”). Cognate to Gujarati જમવું (jamvũ), Konkani जेव्चे (jevce), Marathi जेवणे (jevṇe).

Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *yewg- Proto-Indo-European *-tós Proto-Indo-European *yugtós Sanskrit युक्त (yukta) Prakrit 𑀚𑀼𑀢𑁆𑀢 (jutta) Hindi जुट Inherited from Prakrit 𑀚𑀼𑀢𑁆𑀢 (jutta, “joined”); see there for more. Deverbal form of जुटना (juṭnā).
Borrowed from Sanskrit दुर्जन (durjana). By surface analysis, दुर्- (dur-) + जन (jan).
Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀧𑀲𑀭𑀤𑀺 (pasaradi), from Sanskrit प्रसरति (prásarati). Cognate with Gujarati પસરવું (pasarvũ), Marathi पसरणे (pasarṇe).

s.g: the night or day of the full moon
gift to a superior, a submission, request

ety.text: Borrowed from Classical Persian پیشکش (peš-kaš). By surface analysis, पेश (peś) + कश (kaś).
Borrowed from English fern, from Proto-Indo-European *pornóm. Doublet of पान (pān, “betel leaf”) and पर्ण (parṇ, “leaf”).

Borrowed from Classical Persian بهادر (bahādur). Compare Turkish bahadır. Compare Punjabi ਬਹਾਦਰ (bahādar) / بہادَر (bhādar), Gujarati બહાદુર (bahādur), Marathi बहाद्दर (bahāddar), Bengali বাহাদুর (bahadur), Turkish bahadır, Russian богаты́рь (bogatýrʹ).

Borrowed from Classical Persian بهادر (bahādur). Compare Turkish bahadır. Compare Punjabi ਬਹਾਦਰ (bahādar) / بہادَر (bhādar), Gujarati બહાદુર (bahādur), Marathi बहाद्दर (bahāddar), Bengali বাহাদুর (bahadur), Turkish bahadır, Russian богаты́рь (bogatýrʹ).

Inherited from Sanskrit *विषाधयति (*viṣādhayati, “accomplishes, acquires”), ultimately from वि- (vi-) + साध् (sādh, “to attain, accomplish, acquire”). Compare Nepali बेसाउनु (besāunu, “to buy”), Sindhi विहाइणु (“to buy”), Kumaoni बिसा, बेसा (“purchase of grain”), Old Gujarati विसाहइ (visāhaï, “exchanges”).

ety.text: Inherited from Old Hindi रांणी (rāṃṇī), from Prakrit 𑀭𑀸𑀡𑀻 (rāṇī), from Sanskrit राज्ञी (rājñī), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hrā́ȷ́niH, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rḗǵnih₂ (“queen”). Cognate with Assamese ৰাণী (rani), Bengali রাণী (raṇī), Odia ରାଣୀ (rāṇi), Nepali रानी (rānī), Marathi राणी (rāṇī), Gujarati રાણી (rāṇī), Punjabi ਰਾਣੀ (rāṇī), Romani rani. Distantly related to French reine.

s.g: a female given name, Rani, from Sanskrit

ety.text: Inherited from Old Hindi रांणी (rāṃṇī), from Prakrit 𑀭𑀸𑀡𑀻 (rāṇī), from Sanskrit राज्ञी (rājñī), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hrā́ȷ́niH, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rḗǵnih₂ (“queen”). Cognate with Assamese ৰাণী (rani), Bengali রাণী (raṇī), Odia ରାଣୀ (rāṇi), Nepali रानी (rānī), Marathi राणी (rāṇī), Gujarati રાણી (rāṇī), Punjabi ਰਾਣੀ (rāṇī), Romani rani. Distantly related to French reine.

Borrowed from Classical Persian رُود (rūd), from Middle Persian lwd (/⁠rōd⁠/, “river”), from Old Persian 𐎼𐎢𐎫 (r-u-t /⁠rautaʰ⁠⁠/, “river, torrent”), from Proto-Iranian *hráwtah, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *sráwtas, from Proto-Indo-European *srew-, possibly from *ser-. Doublet of स्रोत (srot).

s.g: a portion of cut crops (payment in kind to harvesters
